extracted.intended_audience: actors, theatre critics, students of acting, and readers of theatrical biography
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating (and producing) stage acting—covering physicality, vocal technique, sincerity, role selection, mobility, and congruence of exterior and interior as illustrated by Edwin Forrest's performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality and muscular realism
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor's physical, muscular display should match the demands of the character; brawny muscularity, terrific indignation, stentorian speech, and merciless revenge were appropriate to the Thracian gladiator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical and muscular vigor is legitimate when it is "sincerity and fitness" to the role. Anti-pattern: condemning necessary, role-appropriate strength as mere 'excess' ignores the historic/physiological truth of the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melodramatic appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Melodramatic or 'physical' acting is acceptable and required when the actual type of man or conjuncture of history demands it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text defends being 'highly "physical" and profoundly "melodramatic"' for parts that historically require it; criticism using 'physical' or 'melodramatic' as slurs is a vulgar prejudice. Anti-pattern: condemning melodrama irrespective of character context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and authenticity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: All manifestations of passion, exertion, and feeling must be sincere and genuinely arise from the actor's nature and the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forrest's strength and passion were 'perfectly genuine and not immoderate by the tests of nature.' Avoid affectation and insincere trickery; genuine force may appear extravagant to some but is valid if authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical training, condition, and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor's bodily condition—training, health, and physical development—contributes fundamentally to the art (e.g., polished skin, quivering musculature, practiced poise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues for popular physical training (gymnastics regulated by music) and admires Forrest's 'muscular coating unified all over him and quivering with vital power.' Guidance: cultivate body as equally sacred as the spirit; anti-pattern: ascetic contempt for the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocal quality and natural declamation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'powerful mellow voice of vast compass and flexible intonation' and declamation modeled on nature is essential to do justice to noble thoughts and beautiful words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid theatrical affectation, whining monotone, and unnatural vocal contortions. Example praise: Mademoiselle Georges's 'rich, full, stirring, and well-modulated tones.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Souplesse (physical and spiritual mobility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brightness, alertness, rich freedom of play in nerves and faculties—the ability to vary, respond, and move with ease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defect identified: Forrest's lack of 'souplesse' robbed him of the 'supreme grace' to achieve large effects with minimal energy. Guidance: strive for quicksilver liberty and rapidity of motion (as Garrick exemplified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of expression vs. excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid both excessive display (overacting for sensation) and deficiency (ponderous heaviness); intensity must be balanced by economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's summary: critics ascribe two faults—an excess (too much display of force) and a defect (lack of souplesse). Excess may be genuine in some natures but can repel delicate sensibilities; aim for appropriate magnitude of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range and variety of emotional expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to present a wide gamut of emotions (stolidity, sorrow, grief, pride, pity, anger, resolution, despair) each well shaded from the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forrest's Spartacus exhibited 'more variety as well as incomparably more freedom and impulsiveness' than Metamora; guidance: develop a broad emotional range suited to the role's civilization/barbarism context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence of exterior and interior (unity of manner and feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exterior movement, gesture, and demeanor must correspond to the character's interior life; the body should reflect the brain (or vice versa) appropriately to the portrayed culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts Metamora (exterior instinctive, body-driven) and Spartacus (exterior volitional, brain-driven). Anti-pattern: mismatch where exterior contradicts interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immersion and transformative embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor should be 'lost in' the character so the audience experiences history resurrected rather than a mere play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Forrest's performance made spectators feel as if witnessing history—'not a play... but a resurrection.' Guidance: create total immersion through port, look, gesture, tone, and sustained conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of manner (port, look, gesture, tone, accent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of physical and vocal manner—posture, facial expression, gesture, tone, and accent—reveals a master-spirit and sways the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combination of these elements can produce a 'signal example of the sovereign potency of manner.' Develop integrated control of all manner elements rather than isolated tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of roles and moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for roles that express 'high-souled manhood' and avoid portraying essentially base or ignoble characters unless to condemn them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forrest disliked trivial, unmeaning roles 'destitute of moral purpose and dignity.' Guidance: select parts that elevate and teach, avoiding association with innovations that detract from purity of the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of pruriency and indecency
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances should be free from pruriency or indelicacy; maintain decorum and moral propriety on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The biography notes that after boyhood Forrest 'could not be induced to appear in any trivial or unmeaning role' and that 'in none of his performances was there ever anything in the least degree savoring of pruriency or indelicacy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness to text and avoidance of theatrical affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Declamation and delivery should be natural and do 'full justice to noble thoughts and beautiful words' without theatrical affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for declamation 'modelled on nature' and criticism of English school anti-patterns: 'snakelike writhing... rolling and straining of the eyeballs... whining monotone.' Guidance: make art 'wholly concealed' so audience forgets the theatre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of manner to teach and move (didactic/ethical impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor's depiction can instruct, elevate democratic/virtuous ideals, and evoke public enthusiasm; performance has social and moral consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forrest's favorite parts 'were expressions of a high-souled manhood' and 'the democratic ideals most wholesome to be cultivated.' Guidance: consider the social and moral import of roles and performance style; anti-pattern: spectacle without moral purpose.
